HREF="#bg79301a_main_toc">Table of Contents</A></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;One
of the principal distinctions among these types of contracts is whether the vessel operator or the customer pays for voyage expenses, which include fuel, port charges, pilot fees,
tank cleaning costs and canal tolls. Some voyage expenses are fixed, and the remainder can be estimated. If we, as the vessel operator, pay the voyage expenses, we typically pass these expenses on to
our customers by charging higher rates under the contract or re-billing such expenses to them. As a result, although voyage revenue from different types of contracts may vary, the net
revenue that remains after subtracting voyage expenses, which we call net voyage revenue, is comparable across the different types of contracts. Therefore, we principally use net voyage revenue,
rather than voyage revenue, when comparing performance between different periods. Since net voyage revenue is a non-GAAP measurement, it is reconciled to the nearest GAAP measurement,
voyage revenue, under "Results of Operations" below. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER" style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><A
NAME="dq79301_significant_events_during_fiscal_2010"> </A>
<A NAME="toc_dq79301_3"> </A>
<BR></FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>  SIGNIFICANT EVENTS DURING FISCAL 2010    <BR>    </B></FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> Goodwill Impairment Charge  </I></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In June 2010, management considered whether or not events or changes in circumstances indicated that the carrying amount of its
goodwill, all of which relates to our Pacific region reporting unit, may not be recoverable. As a result of severe disruptions in our markets causing reductions to our revenue, operating income, and
cash flow forecasts, we determined that such factors were indicative of a triggering event requiring an interim impairment analysis as of June&nbsp;30, 2010. These disruptions in our markets
contributed to a sustained decline in our unit price, and as a result, our equity market capitalization fell significantly below the net book value of the equity. Our goodwill impairment test is based
on a discounted cash flow analysis using the estimated future cash flows from our vessels. The market perceived risk premium implied by our sustained low unit price and increased cost of debt
increased our discount rate causing a full-write off of our goodwill. Accordingly we recorded an impairment charge of $54.3&nbsp;million relating to the goodwill associated with our
Pacific region reporting unit during the three months and year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010. See "&#151;Critical Accounting Policies&#151;Impairment of Goodwill" below. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> Long Lived Assets Impairment Charge  </I></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The expiration of long-term contracts has resulted in increased double-hull availability within the industry.
In addition, the customer preference for double-hull vessels has intensified, resulting in the commercial obsolescence of single-hull equipment. As a result, it is becoming
increasingly difficult to employ single-hull vessels at margins sufficient to operate them profitably. Therefore, although we are permitted to continue to operate our
single-hull tank vessels until January&nbsp;1, 2015, we phased out certain of our single hulls during fiscal year 2010. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During
September 2009, we recorded an impairment charge of $5.9&nbsp;million on certain single-hull vessels based on cash flow forecasts developed using our own data. An
additional impairment charge of $1.7&nbsp;million was recorded during March 2010 relating to four vessels with a net book value of $3.7&nbsp;million. The impairment charge was based on estimated
sales proceeds for such vessels, which were under contracts for sale and which were sold during the fourth quarter of fiscal 2010. We identified a triggering event requiring an impairment review of
all of our long lived assets as of June&nbsp;30, 2010. As a result, an additional impairment charge of $4.2&nbsp;million was recorded relating to eight tug boats, two single hull vessels and one
small vessel used to support activities in Hawaii. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
August 2010, we sold a newbuild 30,000-barrel barge for $2.3&nbsp;million, net of commission and escrow agent fees. As the asset was held for sale as of June&nbsp;30,
2010, we recorded a construction in progress impairment charge of $0.9&nbsp;million reflecting the difference in the purchase commitment cost and the net proceeds received upon sale. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;See
"&#151;Critical Accounting Policies&#151;Impairment of Long Lived Assets" below. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In August 2009, we completed a public offering of 3,244,500 common units representing limited partner interests. The price to the
public was $19.15 per unit. The aggregate net proceeds of approximately $59.2&nbsp;million from the offering, after payment of underwriting discounts and commissions but excluding other transaction
costs, were used to repay borrowings of approximately $35.0&nbsp;million under our revolving loan and credit agreements and to make construction progress payments in connection with our vessel

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> Issuance of Series&nbsp;A Preferred Units  </I></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On September&nbsp;10, 2010, we issued 15,653,775 Series&nbsp;A Preferred Units to KA First Reserve,&nbsp;LLC in exchange for
approximately $85.0&nbsp;million. In addition, KA First Reserve has agreed to purchase an additional 2,762,431 preferred units for approximately $15.0&nbsp;million upon clearance of a
Hart-Scott-Rodino review. The preferred units are convertible at any time into common units on a one-for-one basis, subject to certain adjustments in the event of
certain dilutive issuances of common units. The preferred units have a coupon of 13.5%, with payment-in-kind distributions through the quarter ended June&nbsp;30, 2012 or, if
earlier, when we resume cash distributions on our common units. We have an option to force the conversion of the preferred units after three years if (1)&nbsp;the price of our common units is 150%
of the conversion price on average for 20 consecutive days on a volume-weighted basis,
and (2)&nbsp;the average daily trading volume of our common units for such 20&nbsp;day period exceeds 50,000 common units. The preferred units were priced at $5.43 per unit, which represents a 10%
premium to the 5-day volume weighted average price of our common units as of August&nbsp;26, 2010. We used the net proceeds from the sale of the preferred units to KA First Reserve to
reduce outstanding indebtedness and pay fees and expenses related to the transaction. The preferred units were issued and sold in a private transaction exempt from registration under
Section&nbsp;4(2) of the Securities Act, and certain rules and regulations promulgated under that section. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> Amendment of Partnership Agreement  </I></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Effective September&nbsp;10, 2010, in connection with the issuance of the preferred units to KA First Reserve,&nbsp;the Partnership
entered into the Fourth Amended and Restated Agreement of Limited Partnership ("Restated Partnership Agreement") to, among other things, designate the terms of the preferred units. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
the Restated Partnership Agreement, except with respect to certain matters, the preferred units have voting rights that are identical to the voting rights of the common units and
vote with the common units as a single class, with each preferred unit entitled to one vote for each common unit into which such preferred unit is convertible. The preferred units also have class
voting rights on any matter, including a merger, consolidation or business combination, that adversely affects, amends or modifies any of the rights, preferences, privileges or terms of the preferred
units. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
will not pay any distribution with respect of any common units in any quarter in which the preferred units do not receive a quarterly distribution in full in cash. If we fail to pay
in full any quarterly distribution with respect to the preferred units, the amount of such unpaid distribution will accrue and accumulate from the last day of the quarter for which such distribution
is due until paid in full, and such unpaid amounts will accrue interest at the coupon rate. The record date for the determination of preferred unit holders entitled to receive quarterly distributions
will be the same as the record date for determination of common unit holders entitled to receive quarterly distributions. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
the Restated Partnership Agreement, upon any liquidation and winding up or the sale of substantially all of our assets, the holders of preferred units generally will be entitled to
receive, in </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On August&nbsp;31, 2010, we amended our revolving loan agreement (as amended, "Revolving Loan Agreement") to, among other things,

(4)&nbsp;allow the payment of cash distributions subject to liquidity requirements and certain minimum financial ratios starting with the fiscal quarter ending March&nbsp;31, 2011. The obligations
under the Revolving Loan Agreement are collateralized by a first priority security interest, subject to permitted liens, on certain vessels having an orderly liquidation value equal to at least 1.50
times the amount of the aggregate obligations (including letters of credit) outstanding under the Revolving Loan Agreement. Borrowings under the Revolving Loan Agreement bear interest at a rate per
annum equal, at our option, to (a)&nbsp;the greater of the prime rate, the federal funds rate plus 0.5% or the 30-day London Interbank Offered Rate ("LIBOR") plus 1%, plus a margin based
upon the ratio of total funded debt to EBITDA of between 1.75% and 4.75%, or (b)&nbsp;the 30-day LIBOR, plus a margin based upon the ratio of total funded debt to EBITDA ranging from
2.75% to 5.75%. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B> DEFINITIONS  </B></FONT></P>

</UL>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to understand our discussion of our results of operations, it is important to understand the meaning of the following terms
used in our analysis and the factors that influence our results of operations: </FONT></P>

<UL>
<DL compact>
<DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Voyage revenue.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Voyage revenue includes revenue from time
charters, contracts of affreightment and voyage charters, where we, as vessel operator, pay the vessel operating expenses. Voyage revenue is impacted by changes in charter and utilization rates and by
the mix of business among the types of contracts described in the preceding sentence.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Voyage expenses.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Voyage expenses include fuel and other
items such as port charges, pilot fees, tank cleaning costs and canal tolls, which are unique to a particular voyage. Depending on the form of contract and customer preference, voyage expenses may be
paid directly by customers or by us. If we pay voyage expenses, they are included in our results of operations when they are incurred. Typically when we pay voyage expenses, we add them to our freight
rates at an approximate cost.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Net voyage revenue.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Net voyage revenue is equal to voyage
revenue less voyage expenses. As explained above, the amount of voyage expenses we incur for a particular contract depends upon the form of the contract. Therefore, in comparing revenues between
reporting periods, we use net voyage revenue to improve the comparability of reported revenues that are generated by the different forms of contracts. Since net voyage revenue is a
non-GAAP measurement, it is reconciled to the nearest GAAP measurement, voyage revenue, under "Results of Operations" below.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Other revenue.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Other revenue includes revenue from
bareboat charters and from towing and other miscellaneous services.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Vessel operating expenses.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;The most significant direct
vessel operating expenses are wages paid to vessel crews, routine maintenance and repairs and marine insurance. We may also incur outside towing expenses during periods of peak demand and in order to
maintain our operating capacity while our tugs are drydocked or otherwise out of service for scheduled and unscheduled maintenance.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Depreciation and amortization.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;We incur fixed charges
related to the depreciation of the historical cost of our fleet and the amortization of expenditures for drydockings. The aggregate number of drydockings undertaken in a given period, the size of the
vessels and the nature of the work performed determine the level of drydocking expenditures. We capitalize expenditures incurred for drydocking and amortize these expenditures over 36&nbsp;months.
We also amortize, over periods ranging from three to twenty years, intangible assets in connection with vessel acquisitions.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>General and administrative expenses.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;General and
administrative expenses generally consist of employment costs of shore side staff and the cost of facilities, as well as legal, audit, insurance and other administrative costs. </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Total tank vessel days.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Total tank vessel days is equal to
the number of calendar days in the period multiplied by the total number of tank vessels operating or in drydock during that period.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Scheduled drydocking days.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Scheduled drydocking days are
days designated for the inspection and survey of tank vessels, and identification and completion of required refurbishment work, as required by the U.S. Coast Guard and the American Bureau of Shipping
to maintain the vessels' qualification to work in the U.S. coastwise trade. Generally, drydockings are required twice every five years and last between 30 and 60&nbsp;days, based upon the size of
the vessel and the type and extent of work required. </FONT></DD></DL>
</UL>
<P ALIGN="CENTER" style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>53</FONT></P>

<A NAME="page_dq79301_1_54"> </A>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><A
HREF="#bg79301a_main_toc">Table of Contents</A></FONT></P>

<UL>
<DL compact>
<DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Net utilization.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Net utilization is a primary measure of
operating performance in our business. Net utilization is a percentage equal to the total number of days worked by a tank vessel or group of tank vessels during a defined period, divided by total tank
vessel days for that tank vessel or group of tank vessels. Net utilization is adversely impacted by scheduled drydocking, scheduled and unscheduled maintenance and idle time not paid for by the
customer.  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Average daily rate.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Average daily rate, another key
measure of our operating performance, is equal to the net voyage revenue earned by a tank vessel or group of tank vessels during a defined period, divided by the total number of days actually worked
by that tank vessel or group of tank vessels during that period. Fluctuations in average daily rates result not only from changes in charter rates charged to our customers, but also from changes in
vessel utilization and efficiency, which could result from internal factors, such as newer and more efficient tank vessels, and from external factors such as weather or other delays. </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I>Coastwise and local trades.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;Our business is segregated
into coastwise trade and local trade. Our coastwise trade generally comprises voyages of between 200 and 1,000 miles by vessels with greater than 40,000 barrels of barrel-carrying capacity. These
voyages originate from the mid-Atlantic states to points as far north as Canada and as far south as Cape Hatteras, from points within the Gulf Coast region to other points within that
region or to the Northeast, to and from points on the West Coast of the United States and Alaska, and to and from points within the Hawaiian islands. We also own two non-Jones Act tank
barges that transport petroleum products internationally. Our local trade generally comprises voyages by smaller vessels of less than 200 miles. The term U.S. coastwise trade is an industry term used
generally for Jones Act purposes, and would include both our coastwise and local trades. </FONT></DD></DL>
</UL>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B> Fiscal Year Ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 Compared to the Fiscal Year Ended June&nbsp;30, 2009  </B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B><I> Voyage Revenue and Voyage Expenses  </I></B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Voyage revenue was $248.1&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010; a decrease of $62.3&nbsp;million, or 20.1%, as
compared to voyage revenue of $310.4&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Voyage expenses were $45.9&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, a decrease of
$21.1&nbsp;million, or 31.5%, as compared to voyage expenses of $67.0&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. The decrease in voyage revenue primarily relates to lower utilization
for the fleet. The decrease in voyage expenses primarily relates to lower utilization for the fleet offset by an increase in the price of fuel for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 as compared to
the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B><I> Net Voyage Revenue  </I></B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Net voyage revenue was $202.2&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010; a decrease of $41.2&nbsp;million, or 16.9%, as
compared to net voyage revenue of $243.4&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. In our coastwise trade, net voyage revenue was $160.0&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30,
2010, a decrease of $31.7&nbsp;million, or 16.5%, as compared to $191.7&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Net utilization in our coastwise trade was 79% for the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2010 as compared to 88% for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Net voyage revenue in our coastwise trade decreased by an aggregate $51.7&nbsp;million for the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2010 primarily relating to (1)&nbsp;a decrease of $23.8&nbsp;million relating to thirteen barges which worked in the spot market in the twelve months ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 as
compared to being on time charters during the twelve months ended June&nbsp;30, 2009, (2)&nbsp;a decrease of $11.4&nbsp;million relating to seven single-hull barges, of which three
were sold, three were retired and one was returned to the lessor from a long-term lease in January 2009, (3)&nbsp;a decrease of $10.1&nbsp;million relating to five barges which moved
from transporting petroleum products during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 to performing storage activities for the processing of oily water at our waste water treatment facility during the year
ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, (4)&nbsp;a decrease of $3.1&nbsp;million relating to four vessels on time charter during the twelve months ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009 which had a decline in
average daily rate on their new or renewed time charter, (5)&nbsp;a decrease of $2.3&nbsp;million relating to two vessels which were in the shipyard for an extended period during the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2010 and (6)&nbsp;a decrease of $1.0&nbsp;million relating to one barge which had lower utilization during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 due to weak demand in the spot
market. These decreases were partially offset by an aggregate increase in net voyage revenue in our coastwise trade of $20.0&nbsp;million relating to (1)&nbsp;an increase of $16.4&nbsp;million
due to an increase in the number of working days for our barges due to the delivery of the DBL 76, which began operations in November 2008, the DBL 79, which began operations in January 2009, the DBL
185, which began operations in November 2009, the DBL 54, which began operations in March 2010, and the DBL 106, which began operations in April 2010 and (2)&nbsp;an increase of $3.6&nbsp;million
relating to three barges which were in the shipyard for extended periods during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 and four barges which had higher rates and utilization during the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2010 primarily due to contractual rate increases and some service interruption experienced during the three month period ended December&nbsp;31, 2008. Coastwise average daily rates
decreased 0.9% to $13,340 for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 from $13,457 for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 mainly as a result of lower rates relating to storage contracts serviced by
vessels supporting our waste water treatment facility. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Net
voyage revenue in our local trade for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 decreased by $9.5&nbsp;million, or 18.4%, to $42.2&nbsp;million from $51.7&nbsp;million for the year
ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Local net voyage revenue decreased an aggregate of $10.5&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 primarily due to (1)&nbsp;a decrease of
$2.8&nbsp;million relating to the retirement of three single-hull vessels during fiscal year 2009, (2)&nbsp;a decrease of $3.3&nbsp;million relating to five single hull barges which
were retired during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, (3)&nbsp;a decrease of $3.2&nbsp;million relating to six barges which worked in the spot market in the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 as
compared to being on a time charter for the year ended </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER" style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>55</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='font-family:times;page-break-before:always'></p>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>June&nbsp;30,
2009 and (4)&nbsp;a decrease of $1.2&nbsp;million relating to four vessels which were in the shipyard for an extended period during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010. These
decreases were partially offset by an
aggregate increase in net voyage revenue in our local trade of $1.0&nbsp;million relating to (1)&nbsp;an increase of $0.7&nbsp;million due to a vessel which was placed in service during the
fourth quarter of fiscal 2009, (2)&nbsp;an increase of $0.1&nbsp;million due to one barge which had increased utilization and rates for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 and (3)&nbsp;an
increase of $0.2&nbsp;million due to a vessel that was in the shipyard for an extended period during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Net utilization in our local trade was 74% for the year
ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, compared to 81% for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Average daily rates in our local trade decreased 2.5% to $7,327 for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 from $7,513
for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 due to weak spot market rates. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B><I> Other Revenue  </I></B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Other revenue decreased by $2.7&nbsp;million, or 13.5%, to $17.3&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, as compared
to $20.0&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Other revenue decreased by an aggregate $5.1&nbsp;million due to a decrease of $4.1&nbsp;million due to the expiration of time
charters relating to tug boats acquired in fiscal year 2008 and laying up certain tug boats in fiscal year 2010, a decrease of $0.5&nbsp;million for three barges under bareboat charter during the
year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009, which were disposed in the fiscal year 2009, and the absence of a gain during fiscal year 2010 relating to a customer contract cancellation settlement which occurred
during fiscal year 2009. This decrease was partially offset by an aggregate increase of $2.5&nbsp;million relating to one tug boat towing contract and one barge bareboat contract which each began
during fiscal year 2010. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B><I> Vessel Operating Expenses  </I></B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Vessel operating expenses were $138.1&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, a decrease of $6.2&nbsp;million, or
4.3%, as compared to $144.3&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. Vessel labor and related costs for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 decreased $8.2&nbsp;million, primarily due
to a decrease in crew headcount resulting from lower utilization which was partially offset by an increase in medical insurance costs of $1.5&nbsp;million. Other vessel operating costs decreased
approximately $6.0&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, including: (1)&nbsp;a decrease of $2.1&nbsp;million in repairs and maintenance, (2)&nbsp;a decrease of
$1.7&nbsp;million in insurance expense primarily due to the supplemental insurance call which occurred during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009, reduced premiums relating to vessels sold during
the years ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009 and premium credits for vessels laid up during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, (3)&nbsp;a decrease of $1.3&nbsp;million in outside towing
expenses as a result of additional tug availability during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 due to the retirement of certain single-hull vessels, (4)&nbsp;a decrease of
$0.7&nbsp;million in bad debt expense and (5)&nbsp;a decrease of $0.2&nbsp;million relating to fuel and other costs due to expired towing contracts and a decrease in the overall price of fuel.
These decreases were partially offset by $6.5&nbsp;million of aggregate increases attributable to (1)&nbsp;$5.5&nbsp;million in outside charter fees due to the sale of eight tank barges under
sale leaseback agreements in fiscal year 2009, (2)&nbsp;$0.7&nbsp;million relating to an increase in operating costs for our waste water treatment facility, and (3)&nbsp;$0.3&nbsp;million in
claim costs. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B><I> Depreciation and Amortization  </I></B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Depreciation and amortization was $64.2&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, an increase of $10.6&nbsp;million, or
19.8%, as compared to $53.6&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009. The increase in depreciation and amortization for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 includes $12.6&nbsp;million
due to the impairment of certain vessels and construction in progress as described under "&#151;Significant Events" above. This increase was partially offset by a decrease of
$2.0&nbsp;million for vessels sold under sale leaseback during fiscal year 2009 and lower depreciation for vessels sold and impaired during the years ended June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009. </FONT></P>

June&nbsp;30, 2009 as compared to 87% for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2008. Net voyage revenue in our coastwise trade increased $15.0&nbsp;million for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 due
(1)&nbsp;to an increase in the number of working days for our barges (a)&nbsp;the DBL 77 and the Washington, both of which began operations in July 2008 and (b)&nbsp;the DBL 76 and the DBL 79,
which began operations in November 2008 and January 2009, respectively, and (2)&nbsp;the net decrease in scheduled drydocking days in fiscal year 2009 versus fiscal year 2008. These increases were
partially offset by a decrease of $2.5&nbsp;million relating to two barges that were sold and a decrease of $1.8&nbsp;million relating to a barge which worked in the spot market in the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2009 as compared to being on a time charter for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2008. Average daily rates in our coastwise trade decreased 2.0% to $13,457 for the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2009 from $13,731 for the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2008 due to a write down of our fuel inventory to reflect lower fuel cost and lower rates in the Gulf Coast region due to decreased
demand for #6 oil due to the lower price of natural gas. </FONT></P>

of two vessels from performing operational support activities for our waste water treatment and Philadelphia facilities during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2008 to the spot bunker market in the year
ended June&nbsp;30, 2009 and the return to service of a vessel that was in shipyard for an extended period during the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2008. The $5.8&nbsp;million increase </FONT></P>

ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, 2009 and 2008, respectively. The decrease of $44.5&nbsp;million in fiscal 2010, compared to fiscal 2009, resulted from a $6.8&nbsp;million negative impact from changes
in assets and liabilities, a $1.2&nbsp;million increase in drydocking payments and a $36.5&nbsp;million negative impact from operating results, after adjusting for non-cash expenses
such as depreciation and amortization. During the year ended June&nbsp;30, 2010, our working capital increased, thereby decreasing cash flow, primarily due to an increase in accounts receivable as a

from changes in operating working capital and by decreased drydocking payments of $4.9&nbsp;million, offset by $3.6&nbsp;million of negative impact from operating results, after adjusting for
non-cash expenses such as depreciation and amortization. During fiscal 2008, our working capital increased mainly due to increased accounts receivable as a result of increased revenues,
and increased prepaid expenses as a result of increased fuel inventory which resulted from higher fuel prices. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Oil Pollution Act of 1990.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tank vessels are subject to the requirements of OPA 90. OPA 90 mandates that all single-hull tank vessels
operating in U.S. waters be removed from petroleum and petroleum product transportation services at various times by January&nbsp;1, 2015, and provides a schedule for the phase-out of
the single-hull vessels based on their age and size. At September&nbsp;1, 2010, approximately 90% of the barrel-carrying capacity of our tank vessel fleet was double-hulled in compliance
with OPA 90, and the remainder will be in compliance with OPA 90 until January 2015. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ongoing Capital Expenditures.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Marine transportation of refined petroleum products is a capital intensive business, requiring
significant investment
to maintain an efficient fleet and to stay in regulatory compliance. We estimate that, over the next five years, we will spend an average of approximately $21.4&nbsp;million per year to drydock and
maintain our fleet. We expect drydocking and maintenance expenditures to approximate $20.1&nbsp;million in fiscal 2011. In addition, we anticipate that we will spend approximately
$1.0&nbsp;million annually for other general capital expenditures. Periodically, we also make expenditures to acquire or construct additional tank vessel capacity and/or to upgrade our overall fleet
efficiency. For a further discussion of maintenance and expansion capital expenditures, please read footnote 2 to the table in "Selected Financial Data" in Item&nbsp;6 of this report. The following </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
took delivery of one 30,000-barrel tank barge in July 2010, the DBL 33; and one 30,000-barrel tank barge in August 2010, the DBL 34. These tank barges cost, in
the aggregate and after the addition of certain special equipment, approximately $6.6&nbsp;million. We have a long term contract with a customer relating to the DBL 33. In August 2010, we sold the
DBL 34 for $2.3&nbsp;million, net of commission and escrow agent fees. Since the net proceeds from the sale were lower than the aggregate newbuild cost, we recorded an impairment charge of
$0.9&nbsp;million as of June&nbsp;30, 2010.
We expect to take delivery of a 50,000 barrel tank barge in the third quarter of fiscal 2011 under a lease from the shipyard. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
December 2008, we sold three barges under sale-leaseback agreements with two financial institutions for an aggregate sales price of $34.4&nbsp;million. The proceeds of
the sales were used to make the final payment for construction of one of the vessels, refinance debt with operating lease obligations and fund a security deposit associated with a lease agreement.
Each of the three operating lease agreements gives us the right to renew the lease at the end of its initial lease term, which ranges from ten to twelve years. Two of the leases include early buy out
options after ten years and nine years, respectively. One lease includes a rent escalation after six years. Gains on the sale of two vessels of $0.9&nbsp;million and $0.8&nbsp;million were
deferred and are being amortized as a reduction of lease expense, which is included in vessel operating expenses, on a straight line basis over their respective lease terms. Prepaid rent and deferred
transaction related costs of $1.6&nbsp;million are being amortized on a straight line basis over the respective lease terms. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
June 2009, we sold five barges under sale-leaseback agreements with three financial institutions for an aggregate sales price of $47.8&nbsp;million. Approximately
$34.4&nbsp;million of sales proceeds were disbursed directly by the purchasers to refinance debt with operating lease obligations and fund security deposits associated with certain lease agreements.
Four of the five operating lease agreements gave us the right to renew the lease at the end of its initial lease term, which ranges from nine and a half to ten years. Two of these leases included
early buyout options after nine years, one lease included an early buyout option after seven and three quarter years and two leases included early buyout options after seven years. Gains on the sale
of two vessels of $1.4&nbsp;million and $0.1&nbsp;million are being deferred and amortized as a reduction of lease expense, which is included in vessel operating expenses, on a straight line basis
over each of their respective lease terms. Losses on the sales of two vessels of $0.3&nbsp;million and $0.1&nbsp;million are included in the consolidated statement of operations for the year ended
June&nbsp;30, 2009. Prepaid rent and deferred transaction related costs of $1.1&nbsp;million are being amortized on a straight line basis over the respective lease terms. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Liquidity Needs.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Our primary short-term liquidity needs are to fund general working capital requirements, payment of debt service,
distributions to unitholders, and drydocking expenditures while our long term liquidity needs are primarily associated with expansion and other maintenance capital expenditures. Expansion capital
expenditures are primarily for the purchase of vessels, while maintenance capital expenditures include drydocking expenditures and the cost of replacing tank vessel operating capacity. Our primary
sources of funds for our short term liquidity needs are cash flows from operations and borrowings under our revolving loan and credit agreements, while our long-term sources of funds are
cash from operations, long-term bank borrowings and other debt or equity financings. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
believe that cash flows from operations and borrowings under our revolving loan and credit agreements, described under "&#151;Revolving Loan and Credit Agreements" below, will
be sufficient to meet our liquidity needs for the next 12&nbsp;months. </FONT></P>

<UL>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> Revolving Loan and Credit Agreements</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. </FONT></P>

</UL>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Effective
August&nbsp;31, 2010, we amended (the "Revolver Amendment") our revolving loan agreement (as amended, the "Revolving Loan Agreement") to among
other things (1)&nbsp;reduce the revolving lenders' commitments from $175.0&nbsp;million to $115.0&nbsp;million (subject to a maximum borrowing base equal to two-thirds of the
orderly liquidation value of the vessel collateral), (2)&nbsp;amend the fixed charge coverage and total funded debt to EBITDA covenants and increase the asset coverage ratio , (3)&nbsp;maintain a
July&nbsp;1, 2012 maturity date, and (4)&nbsp;allow us to pay cash distributions subject to liquidity requirements and certain minimum financial ratios starting with the fiscal quarter ending
March&nbsp;31, 2011. In connection with the Revolver Amendment, we incurred amendment and structuring fee totaling $1.16&nbsp;million, excluding other transaction related costs. Due to the
reduction in the borrowing capacity, we will record a charge for the three months ended September&nbsp;30, 2010 relating to a portion of the unamortized deferred costs associated with the previous
revolving loan agreement. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
amended by the Revolver Amendment, the obligations under the Revolving Loan Agreement are collateralized by a first priority security interest, subject to permitted liens, on certain
of our vessels having an orderly liquidation value equal to at least 1.50 times the amount of the aggregate obligations (including letters of credit) outstanding under the Revolving Loan Agreement.
Borrowings under the Revolving Loan Agreement bear interest at a rate per annum equal, at our option, to (a)&nbsp;the greater of the prime rate, the federal funds rate plus 0.5% or 1% above the
30-day London Interbank Offered Rate ("LIBOR") (a "base rate loan") or (b)&nbsp;the 30-day LIBOR, in each case plus a margin based upon the ratio of total funded debt to
EBITDA, as defined in the Revolving Loan Agreement. We also incur commitment fees, payable quarterly, on the unused amounts under this facility. </FONT></P>

 <P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>provided;
that commencing January&nbsp;1, 2011, all pricing associated with a ratio in excess of 6.00:1.00 shall increase by 0.50% and shall continue to increase an additional 0.50% for each fiscal
quarter thereafter for each quarter that such ratio exceeds 6.00:1.00. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest
on a base rate loan is payable monthly over the term of the Revolving Loan Agreement. Interest on a LIBOR-based loan is due, at our election, one, two or three months after such
loan is made. Outstanding principal amounts are due upon termination of the Revolving Loan Agreement. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the Revolver Amendment, the minimum fixed charge coverage ratio will decrease from 1.50 to 1.00 to 0.75 to 1.00 for the fiscal quarter ended June&nbsp;30, 2010; 0.50 to
1.00 through December&nbsp;31, 2010; 0.60 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2011; 0.70 to 1.00 through December&nbsp;31, 2011; 0.75 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2012; and 1.05 to 1.00 through
June&nbsp;30, 2012 and thereafter. In addition, our ratio of total funded debt to EBITDA may not exceed 6.50 to 1.00 for the fiscal quarter ended June&nbsp;30, 2010; 6.90 to 1.00 through
December&nbsp;31, 2010; 6.75 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2011; 6.50 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2011; 5.75 to 1.00 through September&nbsp;30, 2011; 5.20 to 1.00 through
December&nbsp;31, 2011; 4.85 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2012; and 4.40 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2012 and thereafter. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Revolver Amendment limits quarterly cash distributions to our unitholders to $0.45 per unit and requires that, inter alia, we maintain a minimum liquidity of $17.5&nbsp;million in
order to declare any distributions. In general, the Revolver Amendment defines liquidity as the sum of (a)&nbsp;unrestricted cash determined on a consolidated basis plus (b)&nbsp;(i) the lesser of
(A)&nbsp;$115.0&nbsp;million and (B)&nbsp;the orderly liquidation value of the vessel collateral divided by 1.50, minus (ii)&nbsp;the aggregate amount outstanding to the lenders as of the date
of such determination. We will be permitted to pay distributions if (a)&nbsp;the fixed charge coverage ratio is at least 1.0 times for two consecutive fiscal quarters prior to and after giving
effect to such distributions; (b)&nbsp;the projected fixed charge coverage ratio is equal to or greater than 1.0 to 1.0 for the next twelve months and is equal to or greater than 1.0 to 1.0 in three
of four of those quarters; and (c)&nbsp;the total funded debt to EBITDA ratio is less than 5.0 to 1.0. No such cash distributions may be paid prior to the end of the March&nbsp;31, 2011 quarter.
Any decision to resume cash distributions on our units and the amount of any such distributions would consider maintaining sufficient cash flow in excess of the distribution to continue to move
towards lower leverage levels. We will also consider general economic conditions and our outlook for our business as we determine to pay any distribution. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Loan
proceeds under the Revolving Loan Agreement may be used for any purpose in the ordinary course of business, including vessel acquisitions, ongoing working capital needs and
distributions. The Revolving Loan Agreement contains covenants that include, among others: </FONT></P>

<UL>
<DL compact>
<DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>the maintenance of financial ratios (all ratios as defined in the agreement) as shown below;  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>restrictions on creating liens on or disposing of the vessels collateralizing the Revolving Loan Agreement, subject to
permitted exceptions;  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>restrictions on merging and selling assets outside the ordinary course of business;  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>prohibitions on making distributions to limited or general partners of ours during the continuance of a default; </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>prohibitions on making distributions to limited or general partners of ours unless a minimum liquidity of $
17.5&nbsp;million and certain financial ratios are met;  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>restrictions on transactions with affiliates and materially changing our business; and  </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='font-family:times;margin-bottom:-11pt;'><FONT SIZE=2>&#149;</FONT></DT><DD style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>limitations on capital expenditures and permitted acquisitions. </FONT></DD></DL>
</UL>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Revolving Loan Agreement contains customary events of default. If an event of default occurs and is continuing, we must repay all amounts outstanding under the agreement. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
of June&nbsp;30, 2010 borrowings under the Revolving Loan Agreement amounted to $136.0 at the LIBOR rate and $9.0 at the base rate. As of June&nbsp;30, 2009 borrowings outstanding
were $140.0 at the LIBOR rate. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
November&nbsp;30, 2007, we entered into agreements with a financial institution to swap the LIBOR-based, variable rate interest payments on $104.9&nbsp;million of our Revolving
Loan Agreement borrowings to fixed rates, for a term of three years. The fixed rates to be paid by us average 4.01% plus the applicable margin. The fair value of the swap contracts of
($1.9&nbsp;million) and ($4.7&nbsp;million) as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively, is included in other liabilities in the consolidated balance sheets. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
also have a separate $5.0&nbsp;million revolver with a commercial bank to support our daily cash management. On January&nbsp;5, 2010, we amended and restated this revolver. The
amendment reduced the borrowing capacity to $4.0&nbsp;million (subject to a borrowing base limitation of 75% of orderly liquidation value), conformed the financial covenants to the financial
covenants of the Revolving Loan Agreement, including future amendments to such financial covenants, and increased the interest rate margin from 1.4% to 4.25%. Advances under this facility bear
interest at 30-day LIBOR plus the margin. The outstanding balances at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009 totaled $0.0&nbsp;million and $0.4&nbsp;million, respectively. This revolving credit
facility is collateralized by three barges and one tug boat. </FONT></P>

 <P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
October&nbsp;8, 2008, we entered into a loan agreement with a financial institution to borrow $5.8&nbsp;million, for which we pledged two tug boats as collateral. The proceeds of
the loan were used to repay indebtedness under our revolving loan agreement. This loan bears interest at a fixed rate of 5.85% per annum. This loan is repayable by one payment of interest only
covering the period from the closing date through October&nbsp;31, 2008, which was paid on November&nbsp;1, 2008, and 84&nbsp;monthly installments of $0.06&nbsp;million commencing
December&nbsp;1, 2008, with the remaining principal balance of $2.9&nbsp;million, together with interest, due on November&nbsp;1, 2015. Outstanding borrowings were $5.2&nbsp;million and
$5.6&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;5, 2008, we closed the last of eleven fixed-rate term loans aggregating $72.1&nbsp;million, which were entered into between April&nbsp;30, 2008 and
June&nbsp;5, 2008. These loans were arranged with a financial institution, which assigned all but two to other financial institutions. The proceeds of these loans were used to repay borrowings under
our revolving loan agreement, except for $15.0&nbsp;million which was used to repay an advance on such loans which was borrowed on March&nbsp;21, 2008 concurrent with the repayment of a separate
term loan on March&nbsp;24, 2008. These term loan agreements contain customary events of default, including a cross default to our revolving loan agreement, and also the fixed charge coverage ratio
requirement that is included in the revolving loan agreement. In conjunction with the sale-leaseback transactions two of these term loans were repaid in December 2008 and four were repaid
in June 2009. The remaining five term loans have a term of ten years maturing between April&nbsp;1, 2018 and May&nbsp;1, 2018 and are collateralized by three barges and two tugboats. The remaining
five term loans bear a weighted average interest rate of 6.43% and are repayable in an aggregate fixed monthly payment of $0.2&nbsp;million. Final balloon payments on the remaining five term loans
aggregate $9.1&nbsp;million between April&nbsp;1, 2018 and May&nbsp;1, 2018. Borrowings outstanding on these loans totaled $18.8&nbsp;million and $19.7&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010
and 2009, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Also
on June&nbsp;5, 2008, in connection with the acquisition of eight tugboats and ancillary equipment from Roehrig Maritime&nbsp;LLC, we entered into a $31.7&nbsp;million bridge
loan agreement with a financial institution. The bridge loan was to mature on October&nbsp;5, 2008; we have since refinanced $27.5&nbsp;million of the bridge loan with term loans and repaid the
balance on July&nbsp;13, 2008 using our revolving loan agreement. The term loans all have terms of seven years. Two of the loans totaling $19.9&nbsp;million bear a weighted average interest rate
of 6.52% and are repayable in an aggregate fixed monthly amount of $0.2&nbsp;million, with final balloon payments of principal totaling $12.1&nbsp;million due at maturity on July&nbsp;1, 2015. A
third term loan bears interest at LIBOR plus 2.0%, is repayable in fixed principal amounts ranging from $30,896 to $41,946&nbsp;monthly, plus interest, and matures on July&nbsp;1, 2015 at which
time a final balloon payment of principal of $4.6&nbsp;million is due. These term loans are collateralized by six tugboats. Borrowings outstanding on these term loans totaled $24.9&nbsp;million
and $26.3&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;4, 2008, we entered into a credit agreement (the "ATB Facility") with a financial institution pursuant to which the lender agreed to provide financing during the
construction period, and thereafter, for a 185,000-barrel articulated tug-barge unit in an amount equal to 80% of the acquisition costs of the unit, up to a maximum of
$57.6&nbsp;million. Obligations under the ATB Facility were collateralized during the construction period by an assignment of our rights under the construction contract with the shipyard and, after
delivery, are collateralized by a first preferred mortgage in the tug-barge unit and a cash security deposit of $3.1&nbsp;million. Interest is payable quarterly at the applicable LIBOR
rate plus a margin based upon our ratio of total funded debt to EBITDA, as defined in the agreement. The margin ranged from 1.05% to 1.85% through December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2.75% to 4.75% through
June&nbsp;30, 2010. At the November&nbsp;2, 2009 delivery date of the unit, the aggregate of the advances taken during the construction period of $57.6&nbsp;million were converted to a term loan
("ATB Loan") repayable in twenty-eight quarterly payments
covering 37.5% of the term loan, which approximate $0.8&nbsp;million each, plus interest at LIBOR plus the applicable margin. The twenty eighth and final payment will also include a balloon payment
of $36.0&nbsp;million. The ATB Loan contained the same financial covenants as are contained in our revolving loan agreement described above, as well as customary events of default. Outstanding
borrowings were $56.1&nbsp;million and $46.0&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009 respectively, under the agreement. On June&nbsp;13, 2008, we also entered into an agreement with the
bank to swap the LIBOR-based, variable rate interest payments on the outstanding balance of the ATB Loan to a fixed rate of 5.08% over the same term, resulting in a total fixed interest rate of 5.08%
plus the applicable margin. The fair value of the swap contract of ($8.0&nbsp;million) and ($4.6&nbsp;million) as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively, is included in other liabilities
in the consolidated balance sheets. On August&nbsp;31, 2010, we amended the ATB Loan (as amended, "ATB Agreement") to amend the financial covenants in the ATB Loan to conform to the financial
covenants and LIBOR margins in the Revolving Loan Agreement, as amended by the Revolver Amendment. The Revolving Loan Agreement LIBOR margins range from 2.75% to 5.75% and commencing January&nbsp;1,
2011, all pricing associated with a total funded debt to EBITDA ratio in excess of 6.00:1.00 shall increase by 0.50% and shall continue to increase an additional 0.50% for each fiscal quarter
thereafter for each quarter that such ratio exceeds 6.00:1.00. In connection with this amendment, we paid an amendment fee of 0.5% of the outstanding principal amount. At August&nbsp;31, 2010,
borrowings outstanding under the ATB Agreement were $55.3 million. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
February&nbsp;22, 2008, we closed a new ten-year, $5.4&nbsp;million term loan to finance the purchase of a tugboat. The loan bears interest at 6.15%, and is repayable
in monthly installments of $46,220 with a final payment at maturity on February&nbsp;28, 2018 of $2.4&nbsp;million. The loan is collateralized by the related tugboat. The principal balance of the
loan was $4.9&nbsp;million and $5.1&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On August&nbsp;14, 2007, in connection with the acquisition of the Smith Maritime Group, we assumed two term loans totaling $23.5&nbsp;million. The first, in
the amount of $19.5&nbsp;million, bears interest at LIBOR plus 1.25% and is repayable in equal monthly installments of $147,455, plus interest, through August 2018. The second, in the amount of
$4.0&nbsp;million, bears interest at LIBOR plus 1.0% and is repayable in monthly installments ranging from $59,269 to $81,320, plus interest, through May 2012. These loans are collateralized by
three tank barges. We also agreed with the lender to assume the two existing interest rate swaps relating to these two loans. The LIBOR-based, variable rate interest payments on these loans have been
swapped for fixed payments at an average rate of 5.46%, plus a margin, over the same terms as the loans. Borrowings outstanding on the term loans were $16.2&nbsp;million and $18.8&nbsp;million at
June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. The fair value of the swap contract of ($2.1&nbsp;million) and ($1.9&nbsp;million) as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively, is included in
other liabilities in the consolidated balance sheets. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Also
in connection with the acquisition of the Smith Maritime Group, we acquired an option to purchase a 50% interest in a joint venture which was exercised in October 2007. The joint
venture is consolidated in the accompanying financial statements. The joint venture debt, consisting of a term loan which bears interest at 6.5%, matures on October&nbsp;1, 2012, and is
collateralized by the related tank barge. Borrowings outstanding on this term loan at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009 were $1.6&nbsp;million and $2.2&nbsp;million, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
May 2006, we entered into a loan agreement ("Loan Agreement") to borrow up to $23.0&nbsp;million to partially finance construction of two 28,000-barrel and one
100,000-barrel
tank barges. The loan bears interest at 30-day LIBOR plus 1.40%, and is repayable in monthly principal payments of $120,958, plus accrued interest, over seven years, with the remaining
principal amount of $10.3&nbsp;million payable at maturity on June&nbsp;1, 2014. The loan is collateralized by the related tank barges and two other tank vessels. Borrowings outstanding on this
loan were $16.0&nbsp;million and $17.4&nbsp;million at June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. On December&nbsp;30, 2009, we entered into an amendment ("Loan Agreement Amendment") to the
Loan Agreement to amend the Loan Agreement financial covenants to conform to the financial covenants of the Revolving Loan Agreement and incorporate future Revolving Loan Agreement financial covenant
amendments. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
April&nbsp;3, 2006, we entered into an agreement with a lending institution under which we borrowed $80.0&nbsp;million, for which we pledged six tugboats and six tank barges as
collateral. We used the proceeds of these loans to repay indebtedness under our revolving loan agreement. Borrowings are represented by six loans which have been assigned to other lending
institutions. These loans bear interest at a rate equal to LIBOR plus 1.40%, and are repayable in 84&nbsp;monthly installments with the remaining principal payable at maturity. The agreement
contains certain prepayment premiums. Borrowings outstanding on these loans totaled $63.1&nbsp;million and $67.7&nbsp;million as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively. Also on
April&nbsp;3, 2006, we entered into an agreement with the lending institution to swap the one-month, LIBOR-based, variable interest payments on the $80.0&nbsp;million of loans for a
fixed payment at a rate of 5.2275% plus the applicable margin, over the same terms as the loans. This swap results in a fixed interest rate on the loans of 6.6275% for their seven-year
term. The fair value of the swap contract of ($6.7&nbsp;million) and ($6.4&nbsp;million) as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 and 2009, respectively, is included in other liabilities in the consolidated
balance sheets. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
interest rate swap contracts referred to above have all been designated as cash flow hedges and, therefore, the unrealized gains and losses resulting from the change in fair value of
each of the contracts are being reflected in other comprehensive income in the consolidated statements of operations. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On June&nbsp;29, 2010 we entered into amendments to eliminate the financial covenants in two of our operating lease agreements and
one term loan agreement. On August&nbsp;31, 2010, we obtained consents on five operating leases to incorporate by reference the financial covenants in the Revolver Amendment. We incurred fees of
$0.2&nbsp;million relating to such consents. On August&nbsp;31, 2010 the Bareboat Charter was terminated in conjunction with the sale of the vessel by the original lessor to a third party ("New
Lessor"). We were required to pay the original lessor a termination fee of $0.7&nbsp;million. We entered into an eight year operating lease with the New Lessor which requires monthly charter
payments of $0.1&nbsp;million. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Restrictive Covenants.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The agreements governing our revolving loan and credit agreements, the term loans and the operating lease
agreements contain
restrictive covenants, some of which were amended as a result of the amendments and consents described above. The restrictive covenants among other things, (a)&nbsp;prohibit any distributions prior
to March&nbsp;31, 2011, (b)&nbsp;limit quarterly cash distributions to our unit holders to $0.45 per unit and requires that we maintain a minimum liquidity of $17.5&nbsp;million and meet certain
financial covenants in order to declare any distributions, (c)&nbsp;prohibit distributions if a default has occurred and is continuing, (d)&nbsp;restrict capital expenditures, permitted
acquisitions, investments and sales of assets, and (e)&nbsp;require us to adhere to certain financial covenants, including defined ratios of (i)&nbsp;Asset Coverage of at least 1.50 to 1.00,
(ii)&nbsp;Fixed Charge Coverage of at least 0.75 to 1.00 at June&nbsp;30, 2010; 0.50 to 1.00 through December&nbsp;31, 2010; 0.60 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2011; 0.70 to 1.00 through
December&nbsp;31, 2011; 0.75 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2012; and 1.05 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2012 and thereafter, (iii)&nbsp;Total Funded Debt to EBITDA may not exceed 6.50 to 1.00
at June&nbsp;30, 2010; 6.90 to 1.00 through December&nbsp;31, 2010; 6.75 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2011; 6.50 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2011; 5.75 to 1.00 through September&nbsp;30,
2011; 5.20 to 1.00 through December&nbsp;30, 2011; 4.85 to 1.00 through March&nbsp;31, 2012; and 4.40 to 1.00 through June&nbsp;30, 2012 and thereafter (each ratio as defined in the agreements).
As of June&nbsp;30, 2009, we were in compliance with all of our debt covenants. As a result of the August&nbsp;31, 2010 amendments described above, as of June&nbsp;30, 2010 we are in compliance
with all of our financial and debt covenants. Without these amendments, we would have
been in violation of the minimum fixed charge coverage ratio and the total funded debt to EBITDA ratio requirements at June&nbsp;30, 2010. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Issuance of Preferred Units.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On September&nbsp;10, 2010, we issued 15,653,775 Series&nbsp;A Preferred Units to KA First Reserve,
&nbsp;LLC in
exchange for approximately $85.0&nbsp;million. In addition, KA First Reserve has agreed to purchase an additional 2,762,431 preferred units for approximately $15.0&nbsp;million upon clearance of a
Hart-Scott-Rodino review. The preferred units are convertible at any time into common units on a one-for-one basis, subject to certain adjustments in the event of
certain dilutive issuances of common units. The preferred units have a coupon of 13.5%, with payment-in-kind distributions through the quarter ended June&nbsp;30, 2012 or, if
earlier, when we resume cash distributions on our common units. We have an option to force the conversion of the preferred units after three years if (1)&nbsp;the price of our common units is 150%
of the conversion price on average for 20 consecutive days on a volume-weighted basis, and (2)&nbsp;the average daily trading volume of our common units for such 20&nbsp;day period exceeds 50,000
common units. The preferred units were priced at $5.43 per unit, which represents a 10% premium to the 5-day volume weighted average price of our common units as of August&nbsp;26, 2010.
We used the net proceeds from the sale of the preferred units to KA First Reserve, and will use the net proceeds from the sale of any additional preferred units to KA First Reserve, to reduce
outstanding indebtedness and pay fees and expenses related to the transaction. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Issuances of Common Units.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In August 2009, we completed a public offering of 3,244,500 common units at a price to the public of $19.15
per unit. The
net proceeds of $59.4&nbsp;million from the offering, after payment of underwriting discounts and commissions but excluding other transaction costs, were used to repay borrowings of approximately
$35.0&nbsp;million under our revolving loan and credit agreements and to make construction progress payments in connection with our vessel newbuilding program. </FONT></P>


<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
August&nbsp;20, 2008, we completed a public offering of 2,000,000 common units at a price to the public of $25.80 per unit. The net proceeds of $49.8&nbsp;million from the
offering, after payment of underwriting discounts and commissions and payment of expenses, were used to repay borrowings under our revolving loan and credit agreements and to make construction
progress payments in connection with our vessel newbuilding program. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On

public offering of 3,500,000 common units at a price to the public of $39.50 per unit. The net proceeds of $131.9&nbsp;million
from the offering, after payment of underwriting discounts and commissions and expenses, were used to repay borrowings under the revolving loan and credit agreements. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><I> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Conversion of Subordinated Units.</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On January&nbsp;14, 2004, we completed our initial public offering of our common units and, in
connection
therewith, also issued to our predecessor companies an aggregate of 4,165,000 subordinated units. We met certain financial tests described in our partnership agreement for early conversion of the
first 50% of subordinated units and, as a result, 1,041,250 of these subordinated units converted to common units on each of February&nbsp;14, 2007 and February&nbsp;14, 2008. The subordination
period for the remaining subordinated units ended in February 2009 when we met certain financial tests described in our partnership agreement. At that time all the remaining subordinated units
converted into common units on a one-for-one basis. The common units are no longer entitled to arrearages. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B> Seasonality  </B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We operate our tank vessels in markets that exhibit seasonal variations in demand and, as a result, in charter rates. For example,
movements of clean oil products, such as motor fuels, generally increase during the summer driving season. In certain regions, movements of black oil products and distillates, such as heating oil,
generally increase during the winter months, while movements of asphalt products generally increase in the spring through fall months. Unseasonably cold winters result in significantly higher demand
for heating oil in the northeastern United States. Meanwhile, our operations along the West Coast and in Alaska historically have been subject to seasonal variations in demand that vary from those
exhibited in the East Coast and Gulf Coast regions. The summer driving season can increase demand for automobile fuel in all of our markets and, accordingly, the demand for our services. A decline in
demand for, and level of consumption of, refined petroleum products could cause demand for tank vessel capacity and charter rates to decline, which would decrease our revenues and cash flows. Our West
Coast operations provide seasonal diversification primarily as a result of its services to our Alaskan markets, which experience the greatest demand for petroleum products in the summer months, due to
weather conditions. Considering the above, we believe seasonal demand for our services is lowest during our third fiscal quarter. We do not see any significant seasonality in the Hawaiian market. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER" style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><A

<A NAME="toc_dw79301_2"> </A>
<BR></FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>  CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES    <BR>    </B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;An accounting policy is deemed to be critical if it requires us to make an accounting estimate based on assumptions about matters that
are uncertain at the time an accounting estimate is made. An accounting policy is also deemed critical if different accounting estimates that reasonably could be used or changes in the accounting
estimates are reasonably likely to occur
periodically, which changes could materially change the financial statements. We consider accounting policies related to revenue recognition and related reserve, depreciation and amortization of
vessels and equipment, impairment of long lived assets including vessels and equipment and intangible assets, impairment of goodwill, deferred income taxes and loss contingency accruals to be critical
accounting policies due to the judgments and estimation processes involved in each. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2><B> Revenue Recognition and Related Reserve  </B></FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We earn revenue under contracts of affreightment, voyage charters, time charters and bareboat charters. Revenue is generally recorded
when services are rendered, we have a signed charter agreement or other evidence of an arrangement, pricing is fixed or determinable and collection is reasonably assured. We recognize revenue based on
ASC 605, which allocates revenue between reporting periods based on the relative transit time in each reporting period with expenses recognized as incurred. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For
contracts of affreightment and voyage charters, revenue is recognized based upon the relative transit time in each period, with expenses recognized as incurred. We are responsible
for the voyage expenses, which include fuel and other items such as port charges, pilot fees, tank cleaning costs and canal tolls which are unique to a particular voyage, and the vessel operating
expenses, such as wages paid to vessel crews, routine maintenance and repairs, marine insurance, and outside towing. Although contracts of affreightment and certain contracts for voyage charters may
be effective for a period in excess of one year, revenue is recognized over the transit time of individual voyages, which are generally less than ten days in duration. For time charters and bareboat
charters, revenue is recognized ratably over the contract period, with expenses recognized as incurred. For time charters we are responsible for vessel operating expenses, while the customer is
responsible for the voyage expenses. For bareboat charters the customer is responsible for both the vessel operating expenses and voyage expenses. Estimated losses on contracts of affreightment and
charters are accrued when such losses become evident and can be estimated. </FONT></P>

<P style="font-family:times;"><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
extend credit to our customers in the normal course of business. We serve a wide range of customers including major oil companies, oil traders and refiners. We perform a credit review
of all customers with significant transactions to determine whether a customer is credit worthy and collection is probable. Prior credit history with us, credit reports, financial statements, and bank
references are used to assess creditworthiness. We usually do not require collateral. Estimates of uncollectible amounts are revised each period, and changes are recorded in the period they become
known. We provide an estimate for uncollectible accounts based primarily on management's judgment. Management uses historical losses, current economic conditions and individual evaluations of each
customer including the age of its unpaid amounts and information about the customer's current financial strength to make adjustments to the allowance for doubtful accounts. We believe our allowances
to be based on fair judgment and adequate at the time of their creation. Historically, credit risk with respect to our trade receivables has generally been considered minimal because of the financial
strength of our customers. During fiscal 2009 we recorded an increase in the allowance for doubtful accounts of $0.5&nbsp;million primarily due to changes in facts and circumstances relating to an
arbitration proceeding with one
customer. Because amounts due from individual customers can be significant, future adjustments to the allowance may be material if one or more individual customer's balances are deemed uncollectible. </FONT></P>
